results.note: Design, eligibility, capsule placebo, consecutive days, 83-128 mg, completion, 27.8 +/- 8 y, 74.1 +/- 9.2 kg checked (PDF pp. 3-4); no count of women anywhere (limitations say only 'low number of female participants').

Source studies, within-study placebo contrasts, 8 h vs 6 h vital signs, Figure 2 curves (MDMA ends at 6 h, 300 dpi), N per figure/table, power limitation (Discussion 8th para) all match; no MDMA participant characteristics given.

results.corrected_extracted: To check duration, baseline-corrected scores of the five general drug-effect items were examined at 6 and 8 h: no MDMA effect was significantly elevated at 6 h, while MDA raised all five at 6 h and all except bad drug effect at 8 h. At 6 h any drug effect was 41.6 ± 7 points higher after MDA than after MDMA (z = 6.3, p < 0.001) and 46.4 ± 7 higher than its placebo (z = 6.7, p < 0.001); at 8 h it was 35.6 ± 10 above placebo (t = 3.7, p = 0.001). No MDMA values are shown at 8 h in Figure 2 (the methods state a 6-h limit for the MDMA data only for heart rate and blood pressure), so the 8-h comparison is with placebo only.
results.note: All numbers confirmed. 'MDMA was not recorded at 8 h' is an inference: the paper only shows no 8-h MDMA points; a 6-h limit is stated for vital signs, not for the visual analogue items.

results.corrected_extracted: Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (66 items), given 8 h after dosing for retrospective peak ratings, N = 12 per drug, F(3,21): MDA > MDMA (both > placebo) on complex imagery 20.6, elementary imagery 13.9 and spiritual experience 24.8; MDMA > MDA and MDMA > placebo on dread of ego dissolution 15.1, impaired control and cognition 11.1 and anxiety 5.09 (p = 0.008), with no significant MDA–placebo difference listed; audio-visual synesthesia 8.26, with MDA > placebo the only listed difference; both drugs above placebo on oceanic boundlessness 35.9, visionary changes 21.3, blissful state 32.4, insightfulness 19.4, changed meaning of percepts 13.1, experience of unity 17.9 and disembodiment 10.8.
results.note: All 14 F values and pairwise lists confirmed at 300 dpi. 'MDA not above placebo' overstated a non-significant difference (MDA means sit slightly above placebo); page now includes PDF p. 3 for the timing.

results.corrected_extracted: Closeness to others (area under the curve, mean ± SEM): MDA 168.0 ± 53 against its placebo 11.5 ± 38 (MDA > placebo); MDMA 114.4 ± 44 against its placebo −12.5 ± 16 (MDMA > placebo); MDA and MDMA not significantly different; effect of condition F(3,21) = 5.26, p = 0.0073 (printed in a column headed 'Effect of Condition on Emax', although the values are areas). Insightful and new meanings were raised by MDA and did not differ from MDMA. On the interpersonal adjective scale only MDMA increased Affiliation; no statistic is printed, and the text cites Figure 2 for the figure labelled Figure 3.
results.note: Values confirmed. The F placed right after 'not significantly different' could be read as the MDA-MDMA test; it is the overall condition test, in a column headed Emax.

results.corrected_extracted: Main effects of condition on baseline-corrected maximum heart rate (F(3,22) = 17.1), diastolic (32.4) and systolic blood pressure (61.7), all p < 0.0001. Heart rate rose 20 ± 3 bpm after MDA, significantly less than the 30.6 ± 4.5 bpm rise after MDMA (p = 0.03); peak systolic pressure rose 33 ± 2 mmHg after MDA and 31 ± 3 after MDMA; diastolic 24 ± 2 against 19 ± 2 mmHg, a non-significant trend (p = 0.06). Compared with placebo, prolactin rose 16 ± 6 against 29 ± 6 ng/mL (non-significant trend for MDMA higher, p = 0.07) and cortisol 16 ± 1 against 13 ± 2 µg/dL.
results.note: All numbers confirmed; the endocrine rises are stated 'compared to placebo' in the source, a qualifier the anchor dropped.
Abstract sentence and Discussion 3rd paragraph (pressor effects well tolerated in healthy participants, possible concern in cardiovascular disease) match.
Table 1 rows confirmed at 300 dpi; all 11 pages read: no adverse events or follow-up findings reported. Note the F column is headed 'Emax' while rows are areas.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors describe MDA as overall similar to MDMA (for example in raising closeness to others) but with fewer dysphoric effects (lower anxiety and impaired control and cognition), and, qualitatively, as appearing to produce a more introverted and emotionally intense prosocial state, against the more extraverted, gregarious one that MDMA seemed to encourage; this is offered as an impression, with no statistic cited for it.
results.note: Source hedges ('appeared to', 'seemed to'). 'No data are given' is too strong: Figure 3 plots IASR octants (Gregarious, Aloof) without statistics; the authors simply cite none. Passage starts at the foot of the left column.

results.corrected_extracted: MDA and placebo were given on consecutive days, so half the participants had placebo after MDA; MDA and its metabolite were still detectable on the second day; models of placebo sessions only (physiological, endocrine and visual analogue measures) did not suggest significant sequence effects. Limitations stated by the authors: residual next-day MDA may have altered placebo measures in half the participants; comparison with MDMA data from separate studies reduced power; racemic forms only; and a modest sample, a low number of women and single dose levels, which they say prevent full characterization of MDA's pharmacokinetics.
results.note: Facts confirmed; the authors tie the last three limitations specifically to characterizing MDA pharmacokinetics, a scope the anchor dropped.

results.corrected_extracted: MDA elimination half-life 10.9 ± 4 h (mean ± SD; the number analysed is not stated; 12 took part). The MDMA kinetics compared in the discussion are from a separate study, Kolbrich et al. (2008a; 1.6 mg/kg oral MDMA; half-life 8.1 ± 2 h), whose authors include Huestis, an author of this paper, not from the MDMA comparison volunteers. The abstract says the similarity of the two drugs' kinetics points to pharmacodynamics, not kinetics, as the reason for MDA's longer effects; the discussion says the difference in duration may be due to the difference in half-life, or to partly different mechanisms.
results.note: Values confirmed. No n is given for the kinetics; Kolbrich 2008a's last author (Huestis) co-authors this paper, so 'another group's study' is inaccurate.
Introduction, 1st paragraph, left column (PDF p. 2): sentence and both citations match.

Design, registration, random counterbalanced order, washout, 9:00 dosing, room and investigator, sample (14/14, 35 +/- 9.4, 25-52), recruitment, payment, drug history, exclusions and analysed contents (84.5 +/- 0.98 ug; 4.61 +/- 0.09 mg) all on p. 1181.
Table 1 checked at 300 dpi: durations, ranges, F(3,81) = 34.4 and 12.5, onsets; 100 ug LSD onset carries only # (vs psilocybin 30 mg, p < 0.05), while the text claims both LSD doses began earlier.
Discussion 3rd paragraph: 'fully explained' by pharmacokinetics, half-lives ~4 h and 2.5 h, onset attributed to the liquid formulation; no test of the explanation anywhere in the paper.
Results 2nd and 3rd paragraphs and Fig. 2 legend match; 'compared with psilocybin' (emotional excitation) names no psilocybin dose in the source either.
Abstract and Conclusion match; analysis is repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests (p. 1182), and no equivalence testing or margins appear anywhere.

results.corrected_extracted: Both drugs raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature and pupil size compared with placebo; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature significantly more than LSD and psilocybin 15 mg; both LSD doses raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses and placebo; psilocybin 30 mg, not 15 mg, moderately raised heart rate against placebo. Approximate values of the group mean curves in Fig. 3 (editors' reading, not the per-person maxima analysed; peak values and statistics are in Supplementary Table S5, not read): highest systolic about 139 mmHg (psilocybin 30 mg), 134–135 (15 mg), 131–133 (LSD), with placebo about 118–120 over the same hours; heart rate about 81–82 bpm (LSD 200 µg), 76–77 (LSD 100 µg), 72 (psilocybin 30 mg) and 67–68 (15 mg, at 2–2.5 h), with placebo about 62–65 over the same hours; the 15 mg and placebo curves also have an early point at 0.5 h of about 71–72 and 69–70 bpm; temperature highest about 37.65 °C (psilocybin 30 mg) and 37.3–37.4 (other active conditions), with placebo about 36.7 over the same hours.
results.note: Read at 300/600 dpi. Placebo figures are time-matched levels, not placebo peaks (placebo highest ~125 mmHg pre-dose, ~69.6 bpm at 0.5 h, ~36.86 C at 8 h); 15 mg's curve maximum is ~71.7 bpm at 0.5 h, not 67-68.

results.corrected_extracted: Total acute (0–12 h) List of Complaints scores rose with both doses of both drugs against placebo, and subacute (12–24 h) scores with LSD 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg. Adverse events in the evening or within 48 h, by drug (numbers of people): headache 4 after psilocybin and 3 after LSD; migraine 1 (LSD); nosebleed 1 (psilocybin); low mood 2 and 2; nausea 2 (psilocybin) and 1 (LSD); nightmares 1 (psilocybin); restlessness 1 and 1; vivid dreams 1 (LSD); insomnia 1 (psilocybin); involuntary leg movements 1 (LSD). Nine flashback episodes in five people within 72 h (five after LSD, four after psilocybin; a parenthesis says one to 20 times, not explained). No severe adverse events.
results.note: All counts and the LC statements confirmed; the source counts subjects ('four subjects after psilocybin'), so the unit is added to keep events from being read as episodes.

results.corrected_extracted: After the sessions: psilocybin 15 mg named correctly in 64% of sessions (taken for LSD 100 µg in 29%); psilocybin 30 mg in 57% (taken for psilocybin 15 mg in 29%); LSD 100 µg in 57% (taken for LSD 200 µg in 21%); LSD 200 µg in 61% (taken for LSD 100 µg and for psilocybin 30 mg in 18% each). Placebo was correctly identified in 96% of sessions (a sentence that follows the end-of-study results and names no time point). The text says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, and the discussion that the study was well blinded. Editors' calculation (correct guesses plus guesses of the other dose of the same drug): the right drug was named in at least 64%, 86%, 78% and 79% of sessions.
results.note: Percentages confirmed; calculation reproduced (57+29=86, 57+21=78, 61+18=79; 15 mg at least 64). The 96% placebo figure is not tied to the after-session guesses in the source.
Table 1 (300 dpi): 10 +/- 3.1 (6.3-8.8) and 2.5 +/- 0.5 (1.8-2.4); PK text: Tmax 1.6 (1.75-3.0) h. Only Cmax is explicitly called a geometric mean; Tmax follows the same format.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors state a dose equivalence between the two drugs that involves doses not given in this study, reasoning partly from a separate study of psilocybin by the same group; those figures are not recorded here. The analysed LSD content was 11–14% lower than in their earlier studies with the same formulation. Limitations they state: a highly controlled setting and healthy subjects only, so people in other environments and patients with psychiatric disorders may respond differently.
results.note: Each stated equivalence pairs one dose tested here with one not tested; the separate study's dose is not part of the pairs, so 'derived from doses not given' misdescribes it. Other parts confirmed.

p. 237: nine men, word of mouth, paid, 23 y (19-36), >=5 MDMA uses (mean 26, 5-100), prior intoxication, DSM-IV, CYP2D6, smokers, Latin square, 1-week washout, 10-h seated sessions, 350-ml drink, 15 min from 30 min, masking.

Study Design paragraph states the omission and Pacifici 2001; reference list checked: no paper with this trial's cardiovascular data (Mas 1999 is an earlier MDMA study); 'temperature' appears nowhere in the text.
Table 1 rows PCAG, Drowsiness, Drunken match; Fig. 3 read at 300 dpi: drunken about 58 (combination) and 39-40 mm (alcohol), both 'b'; drowsiness about 26 and 8 mm.

results.corrected_extracted: Digit symbol substitution, mean peak differences against placebo: alcohol −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses, combination −4.89 and −8.11; peak correct responses: alcohol vs placebo and combination vs placebo p < 0.01, alcohol vs combination not significant. Over 6 h (area) alcohol differed from placebo (p < 0.01) and the combination did not. Against placebo the impairment lasted 2–3 h with alcohol (from 1 h to 3–4 h after administration) and 1 h with the combination (1–2 h). Reaction decision time at peak: combination vs placebo p < 0.05, the only significant pair; in the time course both alcohol conditions lengthened total and decision reaction time at some time points, the combination for half an hour (1–1.5 h after MDMA). The same sentence of the text says no differences were observed between the two alcohol conditions but that impairment was greater under the combination; Table 1 shows alcohol vs combination not significant.
results.note: Numbers and Table 1 pairs confirmed. The text itself states 'no differences' before 'greater under the combination', so the contrast is within one sentence, not text against table.
Table 2 at 300 dpi matches; recomputed +12.5%, -9.1%, -15.1% (paper 13, 9, 15%); single unit row mg/dl for both drugs; assay range 25-400 ng/ml and MDMA sampling to 10 h confirmed (p. 238).

results.corrected_extracted: The authors say the combination produced a DSST impairment similar to alcohol alone and slightly increased decision time compared with alcohol alone, and that extrapolation to driving is limited; they say the kinetic changes, although statistically significant, are mild in magnitude and could be considered within the range of differences between individuals. They describe a dissociation between subjective and objective sedation, in which people may feel less sedated and feel they perform more efficiently while psychomotor performance stays impaired; they call its road-safety impact unknown and speculate that combined use may potentiate reckless behaviour among drivers. Nobody drove and no rating of one's own performance was taken (the nearest self-rating is the ARCI benzedrine-group scale of intellectual efficiency and energy, which the combination raised above alcohol alone); they say road-safety relevance needs confirmation in field and real-driving studies.
results.note: Source hedges kinetics ('could be considered') and driving ('unknown', 'we could speculate'). 'Perceived performance was not measured' overlooks ARCI-BG (combination > alcohol: area p < 0.01, peak p < 0.05, Table 1).
Results, 8th paragraph, p. 242 left column: sentence content matches.

pp. 1840-1841: design, registration, block randomization, washout, simultaneous dosing at 9:00 after breakfast, 13-h sessions plus 24-h follow-up, sample (12/12, 30 +/- 7, 25-54), drug history, exclusions, analysed contents all match.
Table 1 checked on a rotated 300-dpi rendering: every value and post hoc mark matches; text sentence on temperature (less with MDMA alone) confirmed on p. 1842.
Table 1 List of Complaints, bad drug effect and fear rows confirmed at 300 dpi; p. 1842 sentences on headache, lack of energy, appetite, dry mouth and no severe adverse events match.
All three statements found: p. 1842 (List of Complaints paragraph), Table 1 nausea row (placebo printed '1.0 + 0.7'), Discussion 7th paragraph p. 1845.
Table 2 read on a rotated 300-dpi rendering; all values, CIs and marks match (superscript a = N 23 on MDMA-alone values). Text, abstract, discussion and conclusion mention only LSD's kinetic change.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors attribute the higher LSD exposure to inhibition of the drug-metabolizing enzyme CYP2D6 by MDMA, citing other studies (the discussion says it could be explained this way; the conclusion calls MDMA a blocker of LSD's metabolism); the enzyme was not measured here. They report no indication of greater serotonin toxicity with the combination and say MDMA did not increase LSD's effect on body temperature. Limitations they state: only one dose of LSD and of MDMA; a highly controlled hospital setting; healthy volunteers only, so people in other environments and patients with psychiatric disorders may respond differently; and outcome measures that may not capture all aspects of the experience or very subtle differences between the combination and LSD alone.
results.note: Content confirmed; the limitations list omitted the fourth stated limitation (measure sensitivity), relevant to 'no subjective difference'; 'liver' is not in the source ('metabolic P450 enzyme').

Discussion 2nd paragraph (p. 1844 right column to p. 1845 left): 'might have resulted', 'trend-wise' lower well-being and higher depression on the AMRS, 5 to 12 h, some participants; data only in the supplement.

key_findings.correction: Finding text confirmed; note corrected to: No MDMA values are shown at 8 h (Figure 2; the methods state a 6-h limit for MDMA only for heart rate and blood pressure), so the 8-h result compares MDA with placebo only.

On the visual analogue scales, bad drug effect (area 47.9 ± 26 after MDA, 41.4 ± 16 after MDMA) did not differ significantly from placebo for either drug (effect of condition F(3,21) = 3.1, p = 0.0487, all pairwise comparisons not significant); anxious, relaxed, clear-headed, objects or beings seen with closed eyes and paranoia showed no significant effect of condition. No adverse-event data are reported in the paper. [Relaxed, clear-headed and closed-eye objects or beings are not unwanted effects, so the 'Unwanted effects' heading is dropped.]

MDA pharmacokinetics (mean ± SD; the number analysed is not stated, 12 took part): peak plasma concentration 229 ± 39 µg/L, AUC0–∞ 3,636 ± 958 h·µg/L, elimination half-life 10.9 ± 4 h, clearance/F 30,267 ± 8,214 mL/min. The metabolite HMA peaked at 92 ± 61 µg/L (AUC 1,544 ± 741; half-life 14.1 ± 3 h in the results, 14.1 ± 3.5 h in the discussion), and its peak and AUC varied over seven-fold and four-fold between people.

The authors interpret MDA as having significant entactogen, stimulant and psychedelic effects, and MDMA strong entactogen, modest stimulant and weak psychedelic effects; qualitatively, they say MDA appeared to produce a more introverted, emotionally intense prosocial state and MDMA seemed to encourage a more extraverted, gregarious one, an impression for which they cite no statistic (Figure 3 plots the Gregarious and Aloof octants without tests).

Limitations stated by the authors: MDA and placebo on consecutive days, which may have let residual MDA alter half the placebo sessions; comparison with MDMA data from separate studies, which reduced power; racemic forms only; and a modest sample, few women and single dose levels, which they say prevent full characterization of MDA's pharmacokinetics.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Heart rate and blood pressure were recorded to 6 h for MDMA against 8 h for MDA (Methods), Figure 2 shows no MDMA visual analogue values after 6 h, and the window used for the areas is not stated. | consequence: MDA's larger areas cannot be separated from the unequal observation time; the duration difference rests on the 6-h comparison, since no MDMA data are reported at 8 h. (The abstract's 'resolved by 6 h' is itself supported by the 6-h data.)

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 with an added cross-study domain; overall high is right (consecutive-day carryover, unregistered, unreported outcomes, non-randomized MDA-MDMA contrast). Order allocation is not described here, though the 2010 report of this trial calls it randomized in its title.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. Two phrases in 'claimed' need softening: Kolbrich 2008a is a separate study but shares the author Huestis, so not 'another group's'; the introvert/extravert impression has no statistic cited, but Figure 3 plots related IASR octants, so not strictly 'no data'.

missed: Table 1: MDMA did not differ from its placebo on insightful, surroundings changed, patterns and scenes seen with closed eyes, while MDA did (PDF p. 7); relevant to any MDA-versus-MDMA 'psychedelic-type' contrast.
The paper gives no number analysed for the pharmacokinetics; '12 people' is assumed.
When the ASC was given in the MDMA comparison studies is not stated (8 h after MDA here), so the retrospective peak ratings may not be timed alike.
HMA half-life is 14.1 ± 3 h in the results and 14.1 ± 3.5 h in the discussion (PDF pp. 6, 9); trivial.

key_findings.correction: Course of effects (Table 1; values for 'any drug effect' as predicted by the PK-PD link model, mean ± SD; psilocybin 15 mg, psilocybin 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg): onset 0.8, 0.8, 0.6 and 0.4 h; effect duration 5.6 ± 2.2, 6.5 ± 2.4, 9.3 ± 3.2 and 11 ± 3.7 h (F(3,81) = 34.4, p < 0.001; both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses, p < 0.001); maximal effect 58 ± 25, 80 ± 18, 77 ± 18 and 87 ± 13% of the scale. [Model-derived values must be labelled as such; note unchanged.]

Finding text confirmed; note corrected to: Peak values and statistics are in Supplementary Table S5 (not read). Approximate values of the group mean curves read from Fig. 3 (not the per-person maxima used in the statistics), with placebo given at the same hours, not at its own highest point: systolic highest about 139 mmHg with psilocybin 30 mg, about 134 with 15 mg and about 131–133 with LSD, against about 118–120 with placebo; diastolic about 88, 84 and 80–81 against 73–74; heart rate about 81–82 bpm with LSD 200 µg, 76–77 with 100 µg, 72 with psilocybin 30 mg and 67–68 with 15 mg at 2–2.5 h, against 62–65 (the 15 mg and placebo curves also have an early point at 0.5 h, about 71–72 and 69–70 bpm); body temperature about 37.65 °C with psilocybin 30 mg and 37.3–37.4 with the other active doses, against about 36.7.
Both drugs significantly raised plasma cortisol, prolactin and oxytocin; neither significantly raised BDNF.

Blinding: after the sessions, psilocybin 15 mg was identified correctly in 64% of sessions (taken for LSD 100 µg in 29%), psilocybin 30 mg in 57% (taken for psilocybin 15 mg in 29%), LSD 100 µg in 57% (taken for LSD 200 µg in 21%) and LSD 200 µg in 61% (taken for LSD 100 µg and for psilocybin 30 mg in 18% each). Placebo was identified correctly in 96% of sessions (time point not named; the sentence follows the end-of-study results).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The abstract says 200 µg LSD induced more anxiety than 100 µg; the results text gives a trend (p = 0.054) without naming the instrument, while the Fig. 1 legend says the 5D-ASC anxiety subscale differed significantly. | consequence: Whether the anxiety difference between the two LSD doses was significant depends on an instrument the results do not name; the card should not assign the trend to the visual analogue scales.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns overall is defensible for a registered, randomized, double-dummy crossover with complete data; for the self-rated outcomes, four some-concerns domains plus weak cross-drug blinding sit close to high.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. In 'claimed', the dose-equivalence sentence should say each stated equivalence pairs a tested dose with an untested one, reasoning partly from the group's separate psilocybin study, rather than 'derived from doses not tested'.

missed: can_establish calls the volunteers 'mostly drug-inexperienced', but 18 of 28 had used an illicit drug other than cannabis (each at most 10 lifetime uses) and half a psychedelic (p. 1181); 'with limited drug experience' fits.

End-of-study guesses (p. 1184): 15 mg psilocybin mostly mistaken for 30 mg psilocybin, 30 mg psilocybin for 100 µg LSD, 100 µg LSD for 15 mg psilocybin, 200 µg LSD for 100 µg LSD; cross-drug confusion was commoner at the end of the study, which qualifies reporting issue 3.
The discussion says psilocybin impaired the pupil's light reflex more than LSD (p. 1185); key finding 7 gives only the comparison with placebo.

key_findings.correction: Self-rated sedation (ARCI-PCAG) rose with alcohol alone compared with all other conditions (peak at 2 h, significant from 2 to 4 h); with the combination it stayed at the level of MDMA alone, which the authors describe as MDMA completely reversing alcohol's effect on this scale. MDMA also reduced alcohol-induced drowsiness ratings but did not change feelings of drunkenness, which were raised by both alcohol conditions compared with placebo or MDMA. [Note unchanged. 'So MDMA abolished alcohol's subjective sedation' stated a non-significant difference in 9 people as an abolition.]

The authors call the kinetic changes statistically significant but mild in magnitude, say they could be considered within the range of differences between individuals, and say they may partly explain the effects observed, although a pharmacodynamic interaction might also be possible.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall via the selection domain (unregistered, collected cardiovascular and endocrine outcomes unreported, Table 1 limited to significant variables) is right; other domains fit (Fig. 2 confirms the BG symbols).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible given the authors' hedging. Two fixes in 'claimed': the kinetic changes 'could be considered' within individual variability; and the ARCI-BG self-rating of intellectual efficiency was measured (combination above alcohol), so not strictly 'perceived performance was not measured'.

missed: ARCI-BG (self-rated intellectual efficiency and energy): the combination scored above alcohol alone (area p < 0.01, peak p < 0.05) and above placebo (p < 0.05) (Table 1, p. 239); the nearest measure to the 'feeling of performing better' the authors discuss.
ARCI-LSD (dysphoria and somatic symptoms) rose with both MDMA conditions compared with placebo, slightly more with MDMA alone, peaking at 1 h; alcohol alone did not differ (p. 240; Table 1).

key_findings.correction: Oxytocin: peak changes were 6.0 ± 5.3 (placebo), 289 ± 38 (MDMA), 60 ± 9.0 (LSD) and 286 ± 30 pg/mL (combination); BDNF did not change significantly in any condition (F(3,69) = 0.5).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Three statements on nausea disagree: the results say acute nausea (List of Complaints) was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD; Table 1 shows visual analogue nausea peaks significantly lower with MDMA (7.9) than with LSD (25) or the combination (21); the discussion says nausea was similarly frequent with the combination and with either drug alone. | consequence: On the visual analogue scale nausea was stronger with LSD and the combination than with MDMA; how often it was reported on the List of Complaints cannot be checked without the unread Supplementary Table S6.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns overall fits a registered, randomized, double-dummy crossover with complete data; domain notes check out (placebo recognition indeed absent from the main text; F 4.2 with p < 0.001 recomputed as p = 0.0087).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right; 'claimed' is accurate (oxytocin peaks 286 vs 289; mechanism inferred; nausea contradictions). Editors' percentages recomputed: +10.5%, +35.7%, +33.3%, -10.7%.

missed: On the mood scale, LSD and the combination produced more emotional excitation, introversion, anxiety and depression than MDMA alone (p. 1842; statistics in the supplement).
Pupil light reflex: contraction was smaller with the combination than with LSD alone (0.6 vs 1.2 mm, p < 0.001; N = 23) (Table 1, p. 1843).
The 5D-ASC anxiety subscale was the only 5D-ASC scale not raised by LSD or the combination (trend with LSD, p = 0.073) (p. 1842), relevant to the stated anxiety hypothesis.
